question: The data and the resolution adopted by the European Parliament of 14 September 2023 on the future of the European book sector make clear that timely financial action is needed if the sector is to be saved.

In particular, SMEs in the sector, mainly independent bookshops and publishers, appear to be at risk of closure owing to market challenges, including, for example, generative artificial intelligence and a shortage of financial support. Secondly, publications in regional or minority languages may also disappear, mainly because of the difficulties encountered when attempting to circulate works of those kinds.
In the light of the above: 1.
What action will the Commission take to protect the sector?
Does it plan to support European publications, particularly those concerning the history and traditions of the peoples of Europe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.5.

2024) The Creative Europe Programme1 devotes nearly 8% of the culture strand budget to the book sector through all its horizontal funding schemes2 and sector-specific actions such as a dedicated annual call to support literary translation3 of EUR 5 million; the EU Prize for Literature4, and the Day of European Authors5, a new initiative to promote reading towards young people.
The Programme also supports the whole book value chain from authors and translators to libraries and bookshops or literary festivals.

In addition, policy actions such as the Open Method of Coordination6 – on multilingualism and translation in 2020-2021 and on libraries in 2024 – provide opportunities to discuss with the sector and Member States, as well as offer political orientation on key issues of the book sector.

More specifically, the Creative Europe Programme provides co-financing to publishers to encourage the translation and publication of books, in particular from less represented languages. The financial support covers 60% of the costs linked to the translation, publication, distribution and promotion to a larger audience of European books.

The Commission confirms that national, regional and minority languages recognised in any participating country are eligible. More than 1400 books have been selected for translation since the beginning of the current programme in 2021 involving more than 40 regional, minority or national languages.
